newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Analysts see few hurdles for Westpac bid.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see few hurdles for Westpac bid.

text.p: Westpac Banking Corp's planned takeover of Bank of Melbourne Ltd was likely to get the nod from shareholders and regulators, allowing the Sydney-based giant to increase its share of the competitive Victorian market, analysts said on Thursday.
"I think they would have both done their homework beforehand and I think it will be successful," said Merrill Lynch Australia bank analyst Hayden Aspinall.
"The only chance (of failure) is if someone comes in over the top, but I think that's unlikely."
The friendly bid had been expected since Wednesday when Bank of Melbourne shares first soared suspiciously and trading was then halted ahead of this morning's announcement.

Westpac is confident it can sell the A$1.435 billion bid to the regulators. "We feel very much that this is a pro-competitive merger. We feel we have a very strong case," Westpac managing director Bob Joss told reporters.
But Australian Treasurer Peter Costello, who must approve the deal, said its fate depended on the results of the Wallis inquiry into the financial system.
The inquiry's report is due to be released next week.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), the nation's anti-monopolies watchdog, would also scrutinise the bid.
It has previously said it would not approve a merger that left a state market without at least one strong regional bank.
Analysts said the ACCC would face pressure to approve the bid from others in the finance industry who were also itching to go on the acquisition trail, post-Wallis.
"There's a little bit of punting that pressure will come to bear on the ACCC," said one Sydney analyst, who asked not to be named.

"I would think the chances are that it would let it go through. I think the ACCC is pretty well alone on supporting this...interpretation of the Trade Practices Act. It could well change its view on that," ABN AMRO analyst Michael Pulman said.
Bank of Melbourne let the investment community know it was happy to merge, with chairman Chris Stewart telling reporters: "I think it's extremely good for the shareholders who get a very fair price."

Most analysts also believed Westpac had offered a fair price of A$9.75 per share for Bank of Melbourne, one of the last regional banks in Australia which were characterised by their reliance on home loans and small-medium business lending.
Westpac said it would offer A$8.85 cash and a one-off dividend of 90 cents or one Westpac share plus A$1.85 cash.
Some other analysts, however, said Westpac was buying on the cheap side of expectations.
"The pricing terms seem to be very favourable (to Westpac)," said a Sydney analyst.

"We had (estimated) a takeover price of A$10.42, so it's a little bit below what we were anticipating but it's not that far off," said ABN Amro's Pulman, who calculated the offer before dividend franking at A$10.25.
Analysts said Wesptac would roughly double its Victorian market share and pare its costs considerably.

"(Westpac) gains a good brand name plus there's a very good overlap between the branches and so good cost cutting from branch closures," said Merrill's Aspinall, who put the merged groups's Victorian market share at about 18 percent.
Westpac's Joss said the merger would reap annual cost reductions of between 30 and 40 percent.
"It's realistic. The international benchmark's at about 30 percent," said the Sydney analyst.
-- Melbourne bureau 61-3 9286-1435
